warmup.q: accounts.customer_id is NULL for the 9 merchant and internal accounts. Customer 11 has no account. How many rows does SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts) return?
options: It raises an error because the subquery contains NULL
warmup.why: NOT IN means "not equal to every value in the list". For customer 11 that includes 11 <> NULL, which is unknown, so the whole test is unknown and WHERE drops the row. Customers with an account fail on their own id. Nothing is returned and nothing raises an error. NOT EXISTS returns customer 11.

sections.h: A join pairs rows that match
sections.html:
Payment 17 says card_id 8, merchant_id 4, amount_minor 18999. Support wants a sentence: "Farid Haddad paid Volt Electronics 189.99". The names are not in the payment row, and lesson 2 explained why: each fact lives once, in its own table, and other tables point at it by key. To print the sentence you follow the keys from payments to merchants, and from payments through cards and accounts to customers. Following keys between tables is what a join does.

Here is the simplest way to do it, in Kotlin:

for (p in payments) {
    for (m in merchants) {
        if (p.merchantId == m.merchantId) emit(p, m)
    }
}

That loop is the meaning of a join, and this lesson keeps it as its picture: for each row on the left, look at every row on the right, and keep the pairs the condition makes true. The engine may run it differently (the last section shows how), but the result must be what this loop produces.

Take the if away and the loop emits every pair. That is a cross join: 37 payments times 8 merchants is 296 rows, almost all of them nonsense. Put the if back as an ON condition and you have an inner join:

SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor, m.merchant_id, m.name
FROM payments p
JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id   -- the if
WHERE p.card_id = 8;

p and m are aliases, short names for the tables in this query. JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN. For card 8 it returns four rows, and Volt Electronics appears twice, once next to payment 17 and once next to payment 18. A join copies the right-hand row once for every left-hand row it matches. This is how the flat export in lesson 2 was produced.

So you can predict the size of any join: for each left row, count its matches, and add them up. Every payment has exactly one merchant, because merchant_id is NOT NULL and a foreign key, so payments joined to merchants returns exactly 37 rows. Turn it around and a merchant with 7 payments appears 7 times. Lesson 4 of this track shows how that multiplication breaks sums.

Joins chain. To reach the customer you go payments, then cards, then accounts, then customers, one JOIN ... ON per step, each on a foreign key and the primary key it references. Forget one ON condition and that step becomes a cross join: every row is paired with every row of the next table, and the result is wrong and large.

try.title: Count the pairs
steps: Start the database if needed (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d) and open psql: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.
Predict both counts before you run them: every pair, then only the matching pairs.
Run the five-table join and read off who paid whom for payment 17.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SELECT count(*) FROM payments CROSS JOIN merchants; SELECT count(*) FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id; SELECT p.payment_id, cu.full_name AS customer, m.name AS merchant, p.amount_minor FROM payments p JOIN cards c ON c.card_id = p.card_id JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id JOIN customers cu ON cu.customer_id = a.customer_id JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id WHERE p.payment_id = 17;

try.expect:
The counts are 296 and 37. The chain returns one row:

 payment_id |   customer   |     merchant     | amount_minor
------------+--------------+------------------+--------------
         17 | Farid Haddad | Volt Electronics |        18999
(1 row)

Each step follows a foreign key to the primary key it references, so each step finds exactly one row, and one payment stays one row.

sections.h: Outer joins keep the rows that found no partner
sections.html:
The finance team wants every merchant with its June payments. An inner join answers for four merchants and silently leaves out the other four, because the inner loop found no June payment for them, and an inner join emits nothing in that case. The report must list all eight.

Change one rule in the loop: if the inner loop found no match, emit the left row once anyway, with NULL in every column from the right table. That is a left outer join, written LEFT JOIN:

course=# SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, p.payment_id
course-# FROM merchants m
course-# LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
course-#   AND p.created_at >= '2026-06-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01'
course-# ORDER BY m.merchant_id, p.payment_id;
 merchant_id |        name         | payment_id
-------------+---------------------+------------
           1 | Northwind Grocers   |         34
           2 | Blue Fern Cafe      |         36
           3 | Metro Transit       |         37
           4 | Volt Electronics    |          ∅
           5 | Harbor Hotel        |         35
           6 | Paper Lantern Books |          ∅
           7 | Quick Bite          |          ∅
           8 | Sunrise Grocers     |          ∅
(8 rows)

RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: it keeps unmatched rows of the right table. Nobody needs it, because you can swap the tables. FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

Now the trap. Move the June condition from ON to WHERE and the same query returns four rows, as if you had written an inner join. Lesson 1's logical order explains it. ON is part of the join (step 1, FROM): it decides which payments count as a match, and merchants without a match still get their NULL row. WHERE runs after the join is finished (step 2). By then the NULL rows exist, and for them p.created_at >= '2026-06-01' is NULL >= ..., which is unknown, so WHERE drops them. Every condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN belongs in ON. A condition on the left table, such as m.country_code = 'US', belongs in WHERE.

A join does not need two different tables. customers.referred_by points at another row of customers, so a self join joins the table to itself under two aliases. FROM customers c JOIN customers r ON r.customer_id = c.referred_by pairs each customer with their referrer, and the loop picture still holds: the left and right tables just happen to be the same one.

try.title: Turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner join by accident
steps: Type \pset null '∅'. Run the first query: the June condition is in ON. Count the rows.
Run the second: the same condition, moved to WHERE. Predict the count first.
Run the self join. Which customers were referred by someone from another country?

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: \pset null '∅' SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, p.payment_id FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.created_at >= '2026-06-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01' ORDER BY m.merchant_id, p.payment_id; SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, p.payment_id FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id WHERE p.created_at >= '2026-06-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01' ORDER BY m.merchant_id, p.payment_id; SELECT c.customer_id, c.country_code, r.customer_id AS referrer_id, r.country_code AS referrer_country FROM customers c JOIN customers r ON r.customer_id = c.referred_by WHERE c.country_code <> r.country_code ORDER BY c.customer_id;

try.expect:
The first query returns 8 rows, the second only 4 (merchants 1, 2, 3 and 5). The self join returns four cross-border referrals:

 customer_id | country_code | referrer_id | referrer_country
-------------+--------------+-------------+------------------
           3 | FR           |           1 | IN
           5 | DE           |           1 | IN
           6 | GB           |           3 | FR
          12 | DE           |           7 | SG
(4 rows)

Customers nobody referred do not appear: the self join is an inner join, and r.customer_id = NULL never matches.

sections.h: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS ask whether a match exists
sections.html:
Some questions only ask whether a match exists. Which customers have at least one card? The inner join answers with 14 rows for 11 customers: Ben, Daniel and Ivy each appear twice, because each has two cards and the join emits one row per match. You did not want the cards. You wanted the customers.

SELECT DISTINCT would hide the repeats. It also makes PostgreSQL build every pair first and then sort or hash them away, and it hides the real question in the query text. Change the loop instead: as soon as the inner loop finds one match, emit the left row and stop looking. Emit no columns from the right. That is a semi join, and SQL spells it EXISTS:

SELECT cu.customer_id, cu.full_name
FROM customers cu
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM accounts a
    JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id
    WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id     -- refers to the outer row
);

The inner query mentions cu from the outer query, so it is a correlated subquery: in the loop picture it runs once per customer. SELECT 1 is a convention, because EXISTS looks only at whether a row comes back, never at its columns. The result is 11 rows, each customer once.

The opposite question is just as common. Which customers have no account? Emit the left row only if the inner loop found nothing: an anti join. There are three ways to write it, and only two of them are safe.

NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id) returns Kofi, customer 11. So does LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = cu.customer_id WHERE a.account_id IS NULL, which keeps the NULL-padded rows and nothing else. Test a column that cannot be NULL in a real row, such as the right table's primary key.

WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts) reads the most naturally and returns 0 rows. accounts.customer_id is NULL for the 8 merchant accounts and the internal account, and lesson 1's three-valued logic does the rest. 11 NOT IN (list) means 11 <> 1 AND 11 <> 2 AND ... for every value in the list, including 11 <> NULL, which is unknown. True AND unknown is unknown, and WHERE drops Kofi. One NULL anywhere in the subquery empties the result. The stepper walks through both versions for Kofi. NOT EXISTS asks "is there a row for which the condition is true?", and a NULL row gives unknown, which never counts as a match.

Use NOT EXISTS for anti joins. NOT IN with a list of constants, such as status NOT IN ('failed', 'pending'), is fine, as long as the column itself cannot be NULL.

sections.h: How PostgreSQL finds the pairs without trying them all
sections.html:
The nested loop gives a join its meaning. As a method it is slow. On the course's large data set (schema big, which later lessons load), there are 1,000,000 payments and 2,500 merchants. With the faster methods switched off, PostgreSQL joined just the first 10,000 payments to the merchants by brute force in 0.44 seconds, making 6.3 million comparisons. (It stops at the first match for each payment, because merchant_id is unique.) All 1,000,000 payments would take about 100 times as long, around 40 seconds. Here are the three methods PostgreSQL uses instead, each fixing the previous one's weak spot. The times are from an Apple-silicon laptop under Docker Desktop. Yours will differ with the CPU, but the ratios hold.

First fix: don't scan the inner table, look the row up. merchants has a primary-key B-tree index (lesson 1), so for each payment PostgreSQL can find the merchant by reading a few index pages. That is a nested loop with an index scan. It suits a small outer input. For all 1,000,000 payments it took 265 ms, helped by a small cache of recent lookups that PostgreSQL calls Memoize.

Second fix: build a lookup table once, in memory. A hash join reads the smaller input (2,500 merchants) and puts every row into a hash table keyed on the join column: about 130 kB. Then it reads the payments once, and for each one computes the hash, jumps to one bucket and compares the key there. That is one pass over each input and no index needed. It took 174 ms on one CPU core and 67 ms with two parallel workers. The stepper below shows the build and the probe. Hash joins work only for = conditions, and the hash table must fit in memory (the work_mem setting, 4 MB by default), or PostgreSQL splits the work into batches on disk.

Third method: if both inputs already come sorted by the join key, for example from indexes, a merge join walks the two sorted lists side by side, the way you would merge two sorted Kotlin lists.

The planner picks one by estimating the cost of each, from statistics about your tables, and EXPLAIN shows the choice. Semi and anti joins use the same machinery: NOT EXISTS becomes a Hash Anti Join, which emits a probe row only when its bucket has no match. NOT IN cannot become an anti join, because of the NULL rule. It runs as a filter that checks each row against a hashed copy of the subquery result, called a hashed SubPlan, and when that copy does not fit in work_mem, PostgreSQL falls back to scanning the whole subquery result once per outer row. That is the second reason to prefer NOT EXISTS.

try.title: Read the join method in EXPLAIN
steps: EXPLAIN prints the plan PostgreSQL chose without running the query. COSTS OFF hides the cost estimates so the shape is easier to read.
Run the three statements. Find the join node in each, and which input is under the Hash node.
Compare the NOT EXISTS plan with the NOT IN plan. Which one is a join?

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT p.payment_id, m.name FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id; EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT cu.customer_id FROM customers cu WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id); EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts);

try.expect:
The first plan is a Hash Join with merchants under the Hash node: the build side. The second is a join too:

                  QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------
 Hash Anti Join
   Hash Cond: (cu.customer_id = a.customer_id)
   ->  Seq Scan on customers cu
   ->  Hash
         ->  Seq Scan on accounts a
(5 rows)

The third is not a join at all. It is a scan of customers with a filter: Filter: (NOT (ANY (customer_id = (hashed SubPlan 1).col1))). On tables this small, PostgreSQL picks hash joins almost every time. The Storage track's lesson on indexes and EXPLAIN shows the plans change as tables grow and indexes appear.

video.title: How a database runs a join

analogy: Think of an event with a guest list and a cloakroom. An inner join is the list of coats with their owners' names: guests without a coat are not on it, and a guest with two coats appears twice. A left join is the guest list with a coat column, blank for guests who brought none. A semi join answers "who brought a coat?" and names each guest once. An anti join answers "who came without one?". Now picture a few cloakroom tickets with the name smudged. Asked "is Kofi's name nowhere on the tickets?", an honest clerk says "can't tell, a smudged one might be his". That is NOT IN. NOT EXISTS asks "is there a ticket that clearly says Kofi?", and the answer is no. The analogy breaks at speed: a clerk checks every ticket, while PostgreSQL builds a hash table of tickets once and looks each guest up in one step.
world: Hibernate users meet row multiplication as "my fetch join returns the same order twice": JOIN FETCH o.lines turns one order with three lines into three result rows, and the classic fix is DISTINCT. Now you know why it happens and what it costs. Idempotent Kafka consumers lean on anti joins: "insert the event where NOT EXISTS a row with this idempotency key" (or a unique constraint, which is better still). Older Oracle reports at work may use the (+) outer-join syntax, and every NOT IN (SELECT ...) in them has the same NULL trap in Oracle as in PostgreSQL: SQL defines it that way, so rewrite them as NOT EXISTS when you port them. And when a settlement reconciliation compares two tables, a FULL JOIN on the key followed by WHERE a.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL lists the rows each side is missing in one pass.
mistake: The most damaging join mistake is WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t) where y can be NULL. It works in every test, because the test data has no NULL there, and then returns nothing the day one row with a NULL arrives. No error, just an empty report or a dedupe check that lets everything through. People write it because it reads like English and behaves like NOT EXISTS most of the time. The fix is to write anti joins as NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.y = x), which ignores NULLs correctly and plans as a Hash Anti Join. Keep NOT IN for short lists of constants on columns that are NOT NULL.

compare.title: An outer join in legacy Oracle syntax and in standard SQL

a.label: Oracle (legacy (+) syntax)
a.title: Oracle, old style
a.html: -- (+) marks the side that may be missing SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, p.payment_id FROM merchants m, payments p WHERE p.merchant_id (+) = m.merchant_id AND p.created_at (+) >= DATE '2026-06-01' AND p.created_at (+) < DATE '2026-07-01'; -- leave out one (+) and the outer join -- quietly becomes an inner join

b.label: PostgreSQL 18 (and Oracle 9i or later)
b.title: Standard SQL
b.html: -- the join conditions sit together in ON SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, p.payment_id FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.created_at >= '2026-06-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01'; -- conditions on the outer side go in WHERE

compare.note: Both queries list every merchant with its June payments. Oracle's (+) operator predates the SQL standard's LEFT JOIN and is still accepted, but PostgreSQL does not support it, so ported queries must be rewritten. The rewrite also fixes a class of bugs: with (+), every condition on the optional table needs its own (+), and missing one is exactly the ON-versus-WHERE trap from this lesson. Oracle has accepted LEFT JOIN ... ON since version 9i and recommends it. Semi and anti joins behave the same in both databases, including the NOT IN NULL trap.

worked.title: Customers with no successful payment in the second quarter

steps.say: Marketing wants customers who did not complete a payment between April and June 2026. Start with the positive question, because it is easier to check: which customers did pay? Follow the keys from payments to cards to accounts. Eight customers come back: 1 to 7 and 13.
steps.code: -- 1. the positive set: who paid in Q2 (half-open range from lesson 1) SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id FROM payments p JOIN cards c ON c.card_id = p.card_id JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id WHERE p.status = 'succeeded' AND p.created_at >= '2026-04-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01';

steps.say: The answer is every customer not in that set: an anti join. Move the join chain inside NOT EXISTS and tie it to the outer row with a.customer_id = cu.customer_id.
steps.code: -- 2. the anti join: keep a customer when no such payment exists SELECT cu.customer_id, cu.full_name FROM customers cu WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM accounts a JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id JOIN payments p ON p.card_id = c.card_id WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id -- correlate with the outer row AND p.status = 'succeeded' AND p.created_at >= '2026-04-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01' ) ORDER BY cu.customer_id;

steps.say: Check the answer row by row. It returns five customers, each missing for a different reason: Hugo (8) only has a failed payment in February, Ivy (9) has cards but never paid, Jonas (10) had a payment fail in April, Kofi (11) has no account and Lena (12) has an account but no card. An anti join is right for all five because it asks only whether a matching row exists.
steps.code: -- customer_id | full_name -- -------------+------------- -- 8 | Hugo Silva -- 9 | Ivy Chen -- 10 | Jonas Weber -- 11 | Kofi Mensah -- 12 | Lena Novak

steps.say: Compare a tempting alternative: join everything and keep the customers whose Q2 count is zero. It returns only Hugo and Jonas. Ivy, Kofi and Lena have no payment rows at all, so the inner joins drop them before the count ever runs. A customer with nothing to count is exactly the customer an anti join is for.
steps.code: -- 4. wrong: inner joins remove the customers with no rows to count SELECT cu.customer_id, cu.full_name FROM customers cu JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = cu.customer_id JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id JOIN payments p ON p.card_id = c.card_id GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.full_name HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.status = 'succeeded' AND p.created_at >= '2026-04-01' AND p.created_at < '2026-07-01') = 0; -- returns 8 Hugo Silva and 10 Jonas Weber only

lab.title: An anti join, an outer join and a semi join, checked against the seed
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. All six fail. Each of the three files already holds a query that runs and looks plausible.
never_referred_anyone.sql uses NOT IN and returns nothing. Rewrite it as an anti join with NOT EXISTS.
merchant_failed_payments.sql uses a LEFT JOIN and still loses merchants. Move the condition to where it belongs.
merchants_with_refunds.sql repeats merchants. Rewrite it as a semi join with EXISTS, without DISTINCT.
Run the tests until all six pass. Each exercise has a second test that adds rows first.
hints: SELECT count(*), count(referred_by) FROM customers tells you whether the NOT IN list contains NULLs.
In the loop picture, a condition in ON decides what counts as a match. A condition in WHERE runs on the finished rows, NULL-padded ones included.
The EXISTS subquery needs the refunds joined to their payments, and one condition that ties a payment to the outer merchant.

drill.title: Write the four join shapes from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write four queries over customers cu and cards c (joined through accounts a): every card with its owner's name (inner join); every customer with their cards, keeping customers with none (left join); customers with at least one card, each once (semi join); customers with no card (anti join). Then say which one NOT IN could break, and why.

answer.html: -- inner: one row per card (14 rows) SELECT c.card_id, cu.full_name FROM cards c JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id JOIN customers cu ON cu.customer_id = a.customer_id; -- left: one row per card, plus a NULL row for each customer without one (16 rows) SELECT cu.full_name, c.card_id FROM customers cu LEFT JOIN (accounts a JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id) ON a.customer_id = cu.customer_id; -- semi: each customer with a card, once (11 rows) SELECT cu.full_name FROM customers cu WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id); -- anti: customers with no card (Kofi and Lena) SELECT cu.full_name FROM customers cu WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a JOIN cards c ON c.account_id = a.account_id WHERE a.customer_id = cu.customer_id); -- NOT IN could break the anti join: one NULL customer_id in its list and it returns nothing

recap: A join means: for each left row, look at every right row and keep the pairs the ON condition makes true. Its size is the sum of each left row's matches.
Following a foreign key to a primary key keeps one row per row; going the other way repeats the parent once per child.
A LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs. Conditions on the right table go in ON; in WHERE they drop the NULL rows and undo the outer join.
A semi join (EXISTS) keeps each left row once if any match exists. Use it instead of JOIN plus DISTINCT.
An anti join keeps left rows with no match. Write NOT EXISTS: one NULL in a NOT IN subquery empties the result.
PostgreSQL runs joins as a nested loop with an index, a hash join or a merge join, and EXPLAIN shows which; anti joins appear as Hash Anti Join.

explain.prompt: A teammate's dedupe check, WHERE event_key NOT IN (SELECT event_key FROM processed_events), suddenly lets nothing through after a release added rows with a NULL event_key. Explain what happened and what to write instead.
explain.answer: NOT IN means "not equal to every value in the list". Once the list contains a NULL, the comparison with that NULL is unknown for every incoming key, so the whole NOT IN is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where it is true. Every row is dropped, without an error. NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM processed_events p WHERE p.event_key = e.event_key) asks whether a row with a true match exists. NULL rows never match, so they cannot affect the answer. It also plans as a hash anti join. And event_key should probably be NOT NULL with a unique constraint.

deeper.html:
Joins multiply rows, and aggregates add up whatever rows they get. Put the two together carelessly and totals inflate without any error. Merchant 5 took six succeeded payments worth 335,500 cents. Join in the refunds to show them next to the payments, then sum:

course=# SELECT sum(p.amount_minor) AS paid, count(*) AS rows
course-# FROM payments p
course-# LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
course-# WHERE p.merchant_id = 5 AND p.status = 'succeeded';
  paid  | rows
--------+------
 383500 |    7
(1 row)

Payment 5 has two refunds, so the join returns it twice, and its 48,000 cents are counted twice. sum(DISTINCT p.amount_minor) is not a fix: two different payments with the same amount would collapse into one. The fix is to aggregate each child table on its own first, so every payment or merchant becomes one row, and then join those one-row-per-key results. Lesson 4 of this track, on aggregation, builds that pattern.

Two other join forms are worth knowing by name. JOIN ... USING (merchant_id) is shorthand for ON a.merchant_id = b.merchant_id that also merges the two columns into one in the output. NATURAL JOIN joins on every column with the same name in both tables, which breaks the day someone adds a created_at column to both: avoid it. And a lateral join, JOIN LATERAL, lets the right side refer to the current left row, so it can run a small query per row, such as "this merchant's three largest payments". Lesson 8 covers it.
